opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most exciting shifts happening right now. A lot of the early wins for AI in biology were at the level of individual molecules. Protein structure prediction is the obvious example. You have a sequence, you want a structure, there's a clear ground truth, and there's a lot of well-curated data. That made it a natural first target, and the progress there has been remarkable.

But biology doesn't really happen at the level of a single protein in isolation. Proteins interact with thousands of other molecules, they're expressed differently depending on cell type and state, and the same mutation can have very different effects depending on context. So if you want models that actually help us understand disease or design better therapies, you eventually have to move up the hierarchy, from molecules to cells, then to tissues and organs, and eventually to the whole patient.

What's changed is the data. With single-cell sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and high-content imaging, we now have measurements of millions of individual cells across many tissues and conditions. That's starting to look like the kind of large-scale data that let foundation models work in language and vision. So people are building cell-level foundation models, and increasingly thinking about what a "virtual cell" would look like: a model where you can perturb a gene or add a drug and predict how the cell responds.

I'd add a few cautions, though. At the cellular level, the ground truth is much fuzzier than for protein structure. It's harder to define the right benchmarks, and it's easy to build a model that looks impressive on reconstruction metrics but doesn't actually generalize to new perturbations or new cell types. Some recent evaluations have shown that fairly simple baselines can be surprisingly competitive, which tells us we need to be rigorous about how we measure progress.

And as you go up to tissues and organs, you have to integrate multiple modalities: spatial organization, imaging, clinical data, and so on. That's where I think AI agents and multimodal models become really interesting, not as one monolithic model of everything, but as systems that can reason across different specialized tools and data sources, propose hypotheses, and help design experiments that close the loop with the lab.

So I see it as a natural and necessary progression. Proteins were the proof of concept that AI can learn real biology from data. Cells and organs are where it gets much harder, but also where much of the real impact on medicine will come from.

r001.rationale: It presents protein structure prediction as an early, molecule-level task mapping a sequence to a structure with clear ground truth, characterizing an individual protein as a distinct unit of analysis.

r002.rationale: It connects moving beyond individual proteins to understanding disease and designing therapies, and says cells and organs are where much of AI's medical impact will come from.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. I think it's a really natural and really exciting progression, and in some sense it mirrors how biology itself is organized. Proteins were the right place to start because the problem was so well-defined. You have a sequence, you want a structure, and there were decades of curated data from the PDB. AlphaFold showed that when you have that kind of clean, abundant data and a crisp objective, deep learning can essentially solve the problem. That was a huge proof of concept for the whole field.

But a protein in isolation doesn't really do anything interesting. Biology happens through interactions, through context. The same protein behaves differently in a neuron than in a T cell, and the same cell behaves differently depending on its neighbors and what signals it's receiving. So if we actually want to understand disease, or predict how a patient will respond to a drug, we have to move up in scale to cells, to tissues, to organs.

What's made that possible recently is that the data has caught up. Single-cell sequencing has given us measurements on hundreds of millions of cells across many tissues and conditions, and spatial technologies are now letting us see where those cells sit relative to each other. So you have this foundation for building what people are calling virtual cell models, where the goal is to learn a representation of cellular state that can predict how a cell responds to a perturbation, whether that's a gene knockout or a drug or a change in its environment.

I'd say we're honestly much earlier at this level than we were with proteins. The objective is fuzzier. There's no single ground truth the way a crystal structure is a ground truth. The data is noisier and much more heterogeneous across labs and platforms. And evaluation is a real open problem. We've seen in our own work that some of these cell foundation models don't yet consistently beat fairly simple baselines on perturbation prediction, so there's a lot of hype we have to be careful about.

But I think the trajectory is right. And the piece I find most compelling is that as you move to the organ and patient level, it starts to connect with clinical data, with imaging, with electronic health records. That's where the AI actually becomes useful for medicine rather than just for basic science. So I see it less as leaving proteins behind and more as building the layers on top, and the real challenge for the next few years is figuring out how those layers talk to each other.

r001.rationale: The response says proteins were a well-defined starting point and discusses proteins in isolation, but it emphasizes that their behavior depends on context rather than characterizing an individual protein as relatively self-contained.

r002.rationale: The response connects studying cells, tissues, and organs to understanding disease, predicting patient drug response, and making AI useful for medicine.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a really exciting shift, because proteins don’t operate in isolation. Understanding an individual protein is important, but a cell’s behavior emerges from many different molecules interacting with one another. And when you move to tissues and organs, you also have to understand how different cells communicate and respond to their environment.

So the challenge for AI becomes connecting those scales. Can we go from a change in a protein to predicting how a cell responds, and then how that affects the function of a tissue? That’s a much richer problem than studying any one component.

What makes this particularly interesting is the possibility of moving from describing biological systems to predicting what happens when we intervene. If we introduce a drug or change a gene, what happens downstream? Models that can reliably answer those questions could help us choose better experiments and, ultimately, develop better treatments. But getting there requires testing those predictions against real biological experiments.

r001.rationale: The response says proteins do not operate in isolation and emphasizes interactions, rather than characterizing an individual protein as a relatively self-contained unit of analysis.

r002.rationale: It mentions developing better treatments as a possible benefit, but does not identify human health and disease as the motivation for studying larger biological scales.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a really exciting progression, because proteins don’t act in isolation. They interact with other proteins, with DNA and RNA, and with their environment. So even if we understand an individual protein very well, that doesn’t necessarily tell us what will happen when we perturb it inside a cell.

As we move to cells, the question becomes: Can we model how those interactions give rise to a particular behavior? Can we predict how a cell responds to a drug, or why the same mutation has different effects in different cell types? And then at the tissue and organ level, you have communication between cells and spatial organization becoming important as well.

So I see this as building across scales. The protein models provide useful pieces, but we need ways to connect those pieces to cellular behavior and ultimately to physiology. A key test is whether these models can predict the outcome of new experiments—especially interventions—rather than just describe the data we already have.

r001.rationale: The response says proteins do not act in isolation and that understanding one protein may not predict its effects inside a cell; it does not characterize a protein as relatively self-contained.

r002.rationale: It mentions drug responses, mutations, and physiology, but does not identify human health or disease as a motivation for studying larger biological scales.
